The low-pressure compressor is composed of four stages with 820 airfoils.
The average blade aspect ratio is 2.24 and the average gap-chord ratio is 0.9.
The rotor hub/tip ratios are 0.84 at the inlet and 0.83 at the exit.
The predicted adiabatic efficiency for the Flight Propulsion System is 90.0%.
The predicted adiabatic efficiency for the Integrated Core/Low Spool test is 87.5%.
The inlet corrected airflow is 125.6 lb/sec.
The low-pressure compressor features an adjustable stator 1 to provide flow capacity flexibility for the Integrated Core/Low Spool test.
Controlled diffusion airfoils are used to increase the low loss incidence range capability.
A 15% core mass airflow bleed is incorporated near the low-pressure compressor exit to avoid surge during starting and reverser operation.
The low-pressure compressor rotor for the Integrated Core/Low Spool test uses a bolted steel design rather than the welded titanium design of the Flight Propulsion System.
The low-pressure compressor stator assemblies use non-optimized aluminum cases to reduce design and fabrication costs for the Integrated Core/Low Spool test.
The low-pressure compressor design meets or exceeds all design goals except for surge margin, which is 2% below the 20% goal.
The low-pressure compressor design was not optimized for flight weight, but rather focused on reducing cost and risk for the Integrated Core/Low Spool test.
The low-pressure compressor design retains the aerodynamics of the Flight Propulsion System design while utilizing simplified manufacturing techniques.
The low-pressure compressor rotor critical speeds and mode shapes were analyzed for the Integrated Core/Low Spool test configuration.
